title: Ang 42–53: Guru Arjan
hook: the fifth Guru's Sri Rag hymns
tomorrow: what could possibly rank higher than truth?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fourth guru: Guru Ram Das and his short run of hymns, ang 40 to 42. Turn the page, and the voice changes.

A car that's sat in a parking lot all afternoon in July. You open the door and the heat comes out at you before you've even sat down. You step back, wait, fan the door, swear a little. Some days open exactly like that: the inbox, the group chat, the front door, and a wall of heat. The Granth's next voice has a word for that blast. In his Punjabi it's a taata jhola, a hot gust. So where do you stand when it hits?
screen: `A CAR PARKED ALL AFTERNOON.` → `A WALL OF HEAT.` → `WHERE DO YOU STAND?`

segments.voice: From ang 42 to 53 the Sri Rag hymns belong to Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru and Guru Ram Das's son. His first hymn here opens with a question, in paraphrase: why are you so taken, looking at your children, your partner, your fine clothes? Not because any of them is bad. Because they pass, and he wants your hands on something that doesn't. Two pages on, on ang 44, comes his answer, in paraphrase: O my mind, take hold of the shelter of the Lord's Name, and the hot gust won't touch you. Notice the verb. Take hold, grip, the way you'd grab a railing on a moving bus. Not admire it from across the room. The Name, Naam, is the Sikh word for the presence of the One, remembered until it's right under your hand when you need it. And notice what he doesn't promise. He doesn't say summer ends. He says the heat won't reach you, the way shade doesn't put out the sun; it changes where you're standing. Tradition says this is also the Guru who gathered these very pages into one book. You can hear it in him: say it plainly, then give a picture you can carry. The heat, the shelter, the hand that grips.
screen: `WHY SO TAKEN WITH WHAT PASSES?` · `TAKE HOLD OF THE NAME.` · `THE HOT GUST WON'T TOUCH YOU.` · `SAY IT PLAINLY, THEN A PICTURE.` · then, large: `THE FIFTH GURU.`

segments.voice: Open to ang 44 in a Gurbani app or a steek if one is near, and read one hymn there out loud, slowly, in Gurmukhi or in English, whichever you can. Then rest in the one picture it gave you: the shelter, your hand on it, the heat outside. Let the rest of the sit be shade.
Ang 42. A page of the Guru Granth Sahib, and the page where Guru Arjan's voice enters the first raga.
For the road: the fifth guru, and a shelter to grip when the hot gust comes. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs who read the Guru Granth Sahib in order, at home or at the gurdwara, meet Guru Arjan's Sri Rag hymns, headed Mahala 5, right after Guru Ram Das's; some follow along in a Gurbani app or a steek with the meaning beside each line.

fork.setup: your cousin has three exams, a weekend shift and a phone that won't stop buzzing. she asks for one thing that helps. which fits ang 44?
options: quit the shift. heat is only beaten by getting out of the kitchen.
find one steady thing to grip, a line she can return to between tests.
wait it out. it'll all be over by Friday anyway.
fork.reveal: Guru Arjan's picture is a shelter you take hold of, the Name. the heat comes either way; it just doesn't have to reach you.

original.note: Gurmukhi: ang, a page of the Guru Granth Sahib (the everyday word also means a limb).

what a scholar hears: the hymns headed Mahala 5 mark Guru Arjan; tradition holds that he also compiled these pages into the first Granth.

chat.meaning: On ang 44 the heat still comes, but whoever takes hold of the shelter of the Name isn't touched by it.

Guru Arjan.meaning: the fifth Sikh Guru, son of Guru Ram Das

Sri Rag.meaning: the first raga of the Granth's long run of ragas

Naam.meaning: the Name: the remembered presence of the One

steek.meaning: the Gurbani printed with commentary beside it

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape story (a scene from the listener's world, the hot car, ends on the question 'where do you stand?', which the teach answers with ang 44).

Ang 44 line (man mere gahu har naam kaa olaa, tujhai na laagai taataa jholaa): paraphrased as 'take hold of the shelter of the Name, and the hot gust won't touch you'. Confirm the Ang and the sense of olaa (shelter, support) and taataa jholaa (hot gust).
Ang 42 opening hymn of Sri Rag Mahala 5 (kiaa too rataa dekh kai putr kalatr seegaar): paraphrased. Confirm it is the first Mahala 5 hymn in Sri Rag.
'Tradition says' Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth: standard, hedged on purpose. 'Guru Ram Das's son': standard history; confirm.
The shade image (shade doesn't put out the sun) is the lesson's own picture, not the Guru's; it is framed as a reading.
